question: Which validation-based stopping criterion should be used to stop neural-network training, given a tradeoff between training time and generalization?
hypothesis: Slower stopping criteria (which stop later) give somewhat better generalization than faster ones, at a large cost in training time; no criterion class has a big advantage over another.
contributions: Three classes of stopping criteria (GL, PQ, UP) defined formally
A systematic empirical comparison of 14 criteria on 1296 runs of multi-layer perceptrons on 12 Proben1 problems
Three selection rules for choosing a criterion, and a quantified time versus test-error tradeoff

method.summary: Fully connected MLPs are trained with RPROP on 12 Proben1 problems; each training run evaluates 14 stopping criteria simultaneously (GL, PQ, UP variants) on the same error curve and records when each would stop and the test error of the weights at the validation minimum found up to that point. Results are averaged over all 1296 runs and normalised relative to GL2 or to the best criterion of the same run.
method.task: validation-based early stopping of MLP training (classification and approximation)

datasets.name: Proben1 (12 problems: cancer, card, diabetes, gene, glass, heart, horse, soybean, thyroid; building, flare, hearta)
datasets.size: 8 to 120 inputs, 1 to 19 outputs, 214 to 7200 examples per problem
datasets.split: 50% training, 25% validation, 25% test, drawn in 3 different random ways per problem (36 datasets); the building dataset uses the chronological non-random partition of Proben1
datasets.preprocessing: all inputs and outputs normalised to range 0...1; 1-of-n output encoding for the 9 classification problems

models.name: fully connected feedforward MLP with all shortcut connections
models.architecture: 12 topologies: one hidden layer with 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 or 32 nodes; two hidden layers with 2+2, 4+2, 4+4, 8+4, 8+8 or 16+8 nodes

other.output_units: per topology and dataset, two runs with linear output units and one with sigmoidal output units

training.optimizer: RPROP (epoch/batch learning, weights updated once per epoch), no parameter tuning
training.lr: no global learning rate; RPROP step sizes: initial step per weight drawn at random from 0.05...0.2, max step 50, min step 0
training.lr_schedule: RPROP adaptive per-weight step sizes, increase factor 1.1, decrease factor 0.5
training.epochs: stopped by the criteria; hard cap 3000 epochs; also stopped when training progress P5 drops below 0.1
training.seeds: 3 runs per topology per dataset (two with linear outputs, one with sigmoidal outputs); initial weights random in -0.5...0.5; seed values not given

other.rprop_params_as_printed: eta+ = 1.1, eta- = 0.5 (Greek letters garbled in the text layer, read as RPROP's increase and decrease factors), delta0 in 0.05...0.2 randomly per weight, delta_max = 50, delta_min = 0
other.validation_checking: validation error measured only at the end of each strip of 5 epochs
other.run_count: 1296 runs = 12 problems x 3 dataset variants x 12 topologies x 3 runs
other.records: 1296 runs x 14 criteria = 18144 stopping-criterion performance records

inference.samples: 1296 training runs; all 14 criteria evaluated simultaneously on each run

parameters.criteria: GL1, GL2, GL3, GL5, PQ0.5, PQ0.75, PQ1, PQ2, PQ3, UP2, UP3, UP4, UP6, UP8
parameters.safety_stop: progress below 0.1, or at most 3000 epochs
parameters.returned_weights: the weights with the lowest validation error seen up to the stop

other.deployment_note: in a real application one would add the validation examples to the training set and retrain from scratch for the stopping time found (stated, not run)

metrics.name: slowness S_x(C)
metrics.definition: t_s(C)/t_s(x): training time of criterion C relative to criterion x (x = GL2 or the fastest criterion of the same run that finds the same result, S_Chat)

metrics.name: redundancy r(C)
metrics.definition: (t_s(C)/t_m(C)) - 1: how long training continues after the finally chosen validation minimum; 0 is perfect

metrics.name: badness B_x(C)
metrics.definition: E_te(C)/E_te(x): test error relative to criterion x (GL2 or the best criterion of the same run)

metrics.name: P_g(C)
metrics.definition: fraction of the 1296 runs in which C was a good criterion, i.e. reached the lowest validation error among the 14, however slowly

baselines: best of 14 criteria in the same run (Chat)
eval.protocol: means over all 1296 runs; per problem/criterion means and std over 108 runs shown in Fig 3; no significance test

availability.data: Proben1 benchmark set (anonymous FTP at ftp.ira.uka.de)

results.claim: Selection rule 1: use fast stopping criteria unless small improvements (e.g. 4%) are worth large increases of training time (e.g. factor 4).
results.setup: Rules for setups similar to this study (MLP, RPROP, small datasets)

results.claim: Selection rule 2: to maximise the probability of finding a good solution use a GL criterion; rule 3: to maximise average quality use PQ if the network overfits very little, otherwise UP.

GL criteria are much less robust on the building problem (the only chronologically, non-randomly partitioned dataset); slower criteria are less robust than fast ones for slowness and redundancy, PQ especially on card and horse.
results.setup: Fig 3: per problem mean and spread over 108 runs per criterion

limits: Only one training algorithm (RPROP, epoch learning, small training sets) and one error function (squared error) were used; the author expects similar behaviour for other learners only if they do not take extreme steps (Sec 3.5, speculation).
Only 12 Proben1 problems, none strongly nonlinear; criteria differ by learning problem (Fig 3) and which problem properties cause this is left open.
The author states the discussion is biased by the particular 14 criteria chosen; PQ criteria chosen are slower than the others, so comparing PQ0.5 to GL1 or UP2 is unfair.
The validation set is used only for stopping (never for weight updates); a real application would retrain with it included, which was not tested.
No significance tests or confidence intervals; spread only shown as std over 108 runs in Fig 3.
Theory (Wang et al., Amari et al.) is not applicable to the MLPs and small datasets studied, so the answer is empirical only.
Dated: single-run RPROP MLP setting from the 1990s; nothing on SGD, minibatches, deep nets or large data.

terms.definition: relative increase of the validation error over the minimum-so-far, in percent: GL(t) = 100 * (E_va(t)/E_opt(t) - 1)
stop after first epoch t with GL(t) > alpha
a sequence of k epochs numbered n+1...n+k where n is divisible by k
in per thousand, how much the average training error during the strip is larger than the minimum training error during the strip
stop after first end-of-strip epoch t with GL(t)/P_k(t) > alpha

stop when the validation error increased in s successive strips: UP_s stops after epoch t iff UP_(s-1) stops after t-k and E_va(t) > E_va(t-k); UP_1 stops at the first end-of-strip epoch with E_va(t) > E_va(t-k)
S_x(C)=t_s(C)/t_s(x); r(C)=t_s(C)/t_m(C)-1; B_x(C)=E_te(C)/E_te(x); P_g = fraction of runs in which C was good

code.snippet: GL(t) = 100 * (E_va(t) / E_opt(t) - 1);  E_opt(t) = min_{t' <= t} E_va(t')

P_k(t) = 1000 * ( sum_{t'=t-k+1..t} E_tr(t') / (k * min_{t'=t-k+1..t} E_tr(t')) - 1 );  GL_a: stop at first t with GL(t) > a;  PQ_a: first end-of-strip t with GL(t)/P_k(t) > a;  UP_s: stop when E_va rose over s successive strips

1. Split the training data into a training set and a validation set, e.g. in a 2-to-1 proportion. 2. Train only on the training set and evaluate the per-example error on the validation set once in a while, e.g. after every fifth epoch. 3. Stop training as soon as the error on the validation set is higher than it was the last time it was checked. 4. Use the weights the network had in that previous step as the result of the training run.
